title: Towards greater sensitivity: advancing social life cycle assessment for the coffee sector in Brazil and the Democratic Republic of the Congo
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Literature on coffee sustainability focuses on environmental and economic challenges and often falls short on social factors that strongly influence overall sustainability. For coffee producers, social aspects are existentially important, while environmental concerns take lower priority. Recognizing that social aspects are critical to sustainable development, we assessed the social impacts of nine coffee case studies in Brazil and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Social Life Cycle Assessment (S-LCA) has gained interest and importance to better understand and measure the positive and negative social impacts of products on various stakeholders. However, many challenges in its applicability still exist. Therefore, in this study, we operationalized and applied the S-LCA methodology for the coffee sector, based on the UNEP guidelines and the ISO standard 14,075. We used the reference scale approach based only on primary, site-specific data and systematically involved different actors at the upstream stages of the coffee value chain to capture multiple perspectives. In total, we conducted 170 inventory interviews and included six validation interviews.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We found significant differences in social performance both within and across the two countries; cross-country differences are reported to contrast the two contexts rather than to rank performance. The differences we found within the two countries show that not only context but also organization matters. Especially in Brazil, the cooperative models scored higher than the commercial plantations. In the Brazilian case studies, mean performance scores were highest for the stakeholder category ‘farmer’, followed by ‘local community’, ‘worker’, and ‘value chain actors’. In the Congolese case studies, mean performance scores were highest for the stakeholder category ‘local community’, followed by ‘farmer’, ‘worker’, and ‘value chain actors’. The impact subcategories showing the lowest social performance scores, such as ‘fair salary’, ‘livelihood and well-being’, and ‘productivity’, are the ones that were ranked highest during the validation interviews. We found that workers mostly do not earn living wages, with only seven exceptions in Brazil and one in the DRC.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study contributes to the limited body of S-LCA research on coffee production, and, to our knowledge, is among the first to be based on primary data collected in Brazil and the DRC. It presents a novel approach for achieving greater case sensitivity in S-LCA through primary data and context-specific reference scales, going beyond generic databases. This approach makes it possible to account for differences among case studies within the same country and sector.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Comparative life cycle assessment: environmental impact of beef jerky and its plant-based analogue
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Rising population, income, and urbanisation are increasing demand for animal protein, intensifying environmental pressures associated with meat production. This study evaluates the environmental performance of a plant-based jerky analogue compared with conventional beef jerky, assessing whether a product derived from plant protein blends via high-moisture extrusion can reduce impacts across multiple environmental impact categories.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment (LCA) was performed using the Environmental Footprint 3.1 method to compare beef jerky with a plant-based jerky analogue derived from a plant protein blend. System boundaries covered raw material production, processing, and packaging. The beef jerky inventory was compiled from scientific literature, while primary data from the manufacturer were used for the plant-based product. Background data were sourced from ecoinvent v3.10, Agri-Footprint v6.3, and AGRIBALYSE v3.1 databases. Environmental impacts were assessed across 16 impact categories for two functional units: 1 kg of product and 1 kg of protein. Contribution analysis identified key drivers, and sensitivity and uncertainty analysis evaluated the robustness of the results.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Plant-based jerky showed lower environmental impacts in 15 out of 16 categories for both functional units, with ionising radiation being the only exception. On a product basis, reductions reached 95.0% for climate change and 49.0% for water use. The land-use impact for the plant-based product was negative, which was attributed to the selected characterization method rather than treating it as an absolute environmental benefit. Raw material production was the dominant contributor in both systems. For beef jerky, livestock production drove most impacts, while crop cultivation and protein extraction were the main contributors for the plant-based alternative. Results remained consistent under different sensitivity assessments, confirming robustness. Additional processing stages did not offset the overall environmental advantages of the plant-based product.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The plant-based jerky demonstrates substantially lower environmental impacts than beef jerky across most impact categories, indicating strong potential as a more sustainable alternative. In both systems, raw material production dominates environmental burdens, highlighting the need for targeted upstream improvements to achieve further reductions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Recommendations</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Future research should evaluate the combined usage of multiple plant protein sources and account for the cumulative impacts of additional processing stages. Comparative assessments should also incorporate nutritional factors, including protein digestibility, bioavailability, and conversion efficiency, to enable a more comprehensive evaluation of plant- and animal-based products.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Revisiting microbial supply assumptions: implications of boundary definition for life cycle assessment of bioleaching systems
Consequential life cycle assessment of agricultural products: state of the art and research needs
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Consequential Life Cycle Assessment (cLCA) was developed to assess large-scale consequences, supporting applications like policy-making. Unlike the well-established attributional approach, cLCA is characterized by lower maturity. Specifically, a lack of consensus on the identification of marginal data, system boundary setting and handling of results’ uncertainties impedes its practical use. We examine how agricultural cLCA studies handle these methodological challenges, focusing on food and biobased materials.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A systematic literature review was carried out, initially yielding 229 cLCA studies. The eligibility screening led to the final selection of 23 studies on biobased materials and 32 studies on food. These were primarily analysed regarding marginal data identification, system boundary setting, and uncertainty assessment, alongside supplementary methodological aspects, such as functional unit, use of market models, study scope, and reasoning for consequential modelling.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The review identified a broad variety of approaches for addressing methodological challenges of cLCA, without significant differences between biobased materials and food, while revealing documentation gaps and inconsistencies in reported methodological procedures. Marginal data identification relied mostly on ecoinvent consequential and formalized guidelines, while 11% of the studies did not specify the procedure. Around a third reported using market models or projections. System boundary setting was generally well documented, yet often lacked details, raising concerns regarding the completeness of captured changes. For uncertainty, 25% applied statistical methods and 62% conducted at least a sensitivity analysis, while 22% relied on qualitative discussion only. Further observations included the absence of specifications for temporal scope and justification for consequential modelling.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions and Recommendations</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To improve robustness, cLCA studies would benefit from standardized minimum procedural requirements, for which suggestions from this review can be viewed as a starting point. Specifically, we recommend i) using the JRC (2010) classification as a checklist to qualitatively discuss potential secondary consequences, ii) conducting sensitivity analysis, and iii) explicitly defining the temporal scope. Increased application of quantitative uncertainty assessment would strengthen the reliability of cLCA studies.</jats:p>
                    <jats:p> Future research could test these suggestions in case studies, examine marginal data identification with respect to the practical applicability of existing procedures, and expand the review to biofuels. Overall, methodological harmonization and transparent study documentation are key to increasing the reliability and broader acceptance of cLCA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Advancing silicon die area estimation for integrated circuit modeling in life-cycle assessments
Development of environmental footprint product category rules for Finnish food sector in alignment with Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) method
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to address the pressing need for harmonised life cycle assessment (LCA) practices in the food sector by developing methods that enable comparable, accessible, acceptable, and applicable environmental footprint assessments of food products. Specifically, the study reviewed existing LCA guidelines and Product Environmental Footprint Category Rules (PEFCRs), which were used as a basis to formulate comprehensive methodological guidance for the external communication of environmental information about food products marketed in Finland.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To support the development of methodological guidance for assessing the environmental footprint of food products in the Finnish market, the relevant scientific literature, LCA standards and reports, and policy documents were reviewed. The methods’ adoptability and practical applicability were further assessed based on their data requirements and through consultations with key stakeholders for accessibility and acceptability. Particular attention was paid to four impact categories, climate change, water use, and freshwater, and marine eutrophication, in both the harmonisation of LCA methodologies and the formulation of Finnish Food LCA guidance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Through the methodological review and stakeholder consultations, several inconsistencies, inapplicability, and accessibility issues were identified in the Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) and PEFCR methods, which were subsequently harmonised for the overall Food LCA guidance. Key adjustments included selecting accessible methods for greenhouse gas (GHG) and land use and land use change (LULUC) emissions, omitting circular footprint formula (CFF) due to its complexity and deviation from the attributional approach, recommending only economic allocation, replacing the functional unit with the declared unit to ensure applicability across all food products, clarifying water scarcity and eutrophication assessment, and including an approach for eutrophication assessment in Baltic Sea conditions, and providing detailed guidance on peat modelling.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study identified several inconsistencies in current approaches and highlighted broader development needs for enhancing the harmonisation of food LCAs and the European Commission’s PEF method, including needs for standardised methods for animal production emissions, improved modelling of soil carbon, crop sequences, and organic fertilisers, region-specific eutrophication models, integration of social and economic sustainability dimensions, and clear guidance on the inclusion of nutritional aspects to enable fair product comparisons while avoiding greenwashing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Environmental evaluation of plastic waste end-of-life pathways in Malang District, Indonesia: a life cycle approach
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Malang is an Indonesian District struggling with waste management: low collection rates, fly-tipping, and burning. This study conducts a Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) on the end-of-life pathways of plastic waste (PW) in Malang. All the stages of the PW management system are covered, from PW generation and transportation to unregulated and regulated PW management strategies. Ultimately, the findings aim to support policymakers in understanding the environmental impact of PW management and how to mitigate it.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Stakeholder interviews provided primary data, which informed the Life Cycle Inventory (LCI) across all stages of the PW management system in villages of Malang District. The data was then adapted into the functional unit (FU) of 1 kg of PW generated and statistically analysed to understand PW end-of-life trends. The LCA was conducted using the open-source software Activity Browser. In this case, the ReCiPe v1.03 midpoint impact categories considered were global warming, primary energy depletion, and particulate matter formation. The results of the analysed villages were compared with the national average. The PW from four villages (Bakalan, Krebet Senggrong, Krebet, and Tlogorejo) were modelled under three end-of-life scenarios i.e., landfilling, recycling, and incineration with energy recovery to inform intervention selection.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In the baseline scenarios of the villages, the highest impact in Global Warming Potential, Fossil Fuel Potential, and Particulate Matter Formation Potential (GWP100, FFP, and PMFP, respectively) was linked to higher rates of open burning (e.g., Krebet Senggrong where 35% of waste is open burned). Villages with the highest recycling rates however present lower GWP100 and FFP, such as the case of Bedali and Mangunrejo, where 16.6% and 14.3% of plastic is recycled, respectively. Low PMFP is tied to options such as landfilling, which occurred in Rekasan. The alternative intervention strategy with the lowest environmental impact is recycling (when considering avoided plastic production, GWP100 and FFP are negative). However, it is the alternative with the highest PMFP, even surpassing the baseline scenario.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Open burning remains one of the most prevalent PW management strategies in Malang, which is not only detrimental to the environment but also proven to negatively impact human health, particularly respiratory health. It is essential not only to increase waste collection and treatment rates, but also to ensure that waste‑management practices meet environmental standards and minimise adverse impacts on human health and the environment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Assessment of GHG emission reduction potential of an integrated community solar and biogas renewable energy system: a case study of Hakwata Green Village in Zimbabwe
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study analyses the greenhouse gas (GHG) emission impact of a combined community solar and biogas energy system, using the Hakwata Green Village in Zimbabwe as a case study. The primary aim is to evaluate the Global Warming Potential (GWP) reduction for carbon finance achieved by a 200 kWp/915 kWh solar mini-grid and a 540 m³ biogas plant serving over 12 500 people, relative to default alternatives (grid extension for solar; firewood for biogas).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A comprehensive Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) was conducted using SimaPro with the ReCiPe 2016 method, focusing on GWP as the key climate change driver and role in carbon finance. The study employs a dual functional unit system: kWh of electricity delivered from the solar mini grid and MJ of energy delivered from the biogas system over the project’s 20-year life. Avoided emissions were calculated from the replacement of national grid with solar, firewood with biogas and the replacement of synthetic fertiliser with biogas digestate.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The solar PV system exhibits a life-cycle emission intensity of 145 g CO₂ eq kWh⁻¹, an 85% reduction compared to the Southern African Power Pool grid (SAPP) mix (980 g CO₂ eq kWh⁻¹). The biogas system, despite construction phase emissions, achieves a net negative carbon balance of 26,851.90 t CO₂ eq over 20 years once avoided firewood and synthetic fertiliser burdens are credited. When the two subsystems are combined and compared with the baseline, the integrated community energy system reduces GWP by 1,614 t CO₂ eq year⁻¹, yielding a cumulative net reduction of 33,408 t CO₂ eq over the 20-year project life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings confirm that an integrated solar-biogas community energy system can deliver emission reductions of 8% against grid electricity and 9% against firewood, while avoiding 33,408 t CO₂ eq over 20 years. These verified reductions, combined with improved energy access, make such projects are strong candidates for carbon finance, offering a replicable rural electrification model beyond the Hakwata Green Village case.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Interoperability of uncertainty information in LCI databases
A global consensus life cycle impact assessment method - GLAM: impacts on ecosystem quality
Transparent and harmonized allocation factors for crop-processing co-products in U.S. dairy rations
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Crop-processing co-products are widely used in U.S. dairy rations and contribute substantially to feed supply, yet the allocation factors needed to assign them a share of upstream crop-production burdens are not harmonized across methods or available in a single transparent resource.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study compiled a database of economic, dry-matter mass, and gross energy allocation factors for 62 dairy-relevant co-products from 22 U.S. plant-processing systems, including small grains, oilseeds, sugar crops, vegetables, and specialty crops, derived from explicit equations applied to harmonized inventory data for 2024–2025. Parametric uncertainty was quantified using Monte Carlo simulation with 10,000 iterations per system and Program Evaluation and Review Technique (PERT) distributed inputs for co-product yields, market prices, and gross energy content, and a cross-method divergence index was used to characterize sensitivity to allocation choice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of the 62 co-products evaluated, 29 were classified as high sensitivity, 22 as moderate, and 11 as low, with the greatest divergence occurring in almond, sweet corn, citrus, peanut, cotton, and safflower systems. For most co-products, variation across allocation methods exceeded parametric uncertainty within any single method, indicating that allocation choice is the main source of methodological variability in co-product environmental assessment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The resulting factors are impact-category neutral and designed to interface with any upstream crop life-cycle inventory, complementing rather than replacing allocations already embedded in general-purpose life-cycle inventory databases.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Consensus-based framework for the impact assessment of natural resource use in life cycle assessment: generalized impact pathways and recommended methods for abiotic resource use
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to establish a consistent framework for assessing the impacts of natural resource use within Life Cycle Assessment (LCA). As part of the outcomes of the UNEP Life Cycle Initiative’s GLAM Phase 3 Task Force on Natural Resources, the work defines the safeguard subject, generalized impact pathways applicable across all types of natural resources, and recommended methods for abiotic resource use that aligns with the developed assessment framework for natural resources.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An expert consensus was achieved through a structured evaluation of twenty existing methods using ten criteria, including relevance to the defined safeguard subject, consistency with impact pathways, data quality, and compatibility with Life Cycle Inventory (LCI) databases. The generalized impact pathways were developed to encompass abiotic, biotic and other renewable resources, integrating mechanisms such as dissipation, degradation, and occupation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The consensus-building process resulted in the definition of a common safeguard subject for natural resource use: the potential to make use of the instrumental values of natural resources. Generalized impact pathways were established to consistently describe cause-effect mechanisms across different categories of natural resources. The Future Welfare Loss (FWL) model was selected as the recommended approach for assessing mineral and fossil resource use. Characterization factors (CFs) were recalculated using updated 2018 commodity price data for 81 minerals, 3 fossil resources, and 2 energy carriers. The global annual impact of mineral and fossil resource use (using extraction flows as inputs) was estimated at approximately USD 3,483 billion, equivalent to about 4% of the 2018 global GDP.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While the generalized impact pathways are intended to be broadly applicable across natural resource categories, the operational recommendation and updated characterization factors currently focus on mineral and fossil resource use, whereas only interim recommendations could be identified for water resource use and land use assessment. Further methodological refinement is needed for renewable resources. Finally, we encourage LCI databases developers to improve the coverage of mineral and fossil resource dissipative flows in LCI databases to enhance the characterization of resource dissipation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Carbon footprint and carbon-related costs of LFP and NMC811 traction battery packs in China – a pack-level life-cycle assessment under trade-weighted carbon price exposure
Appetite-based functional units for food life cycle assessment: integrating experimental measures of satiety and satiation

A V-model for LCA: scheduling life cycle assessment within product development
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As of today, Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) is a process that is still largely separated from product development processes. Acknowledging the increasing necessity for sustainable product development amidst stringent regulatory and consumer demands, integration of LCA into product development processes is necessary to ensure efficient ecodesign practices.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this paper a methodology integrating Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) into methods of product development, specifically the V-model is used to schedule LCA in product development processes. The methodology identifies critical data needs and sources relevant to LCA, ensuring a scheduled integration of sustainability metrics into the existing V-model for product development. A V-model structure for LCA studies is provided to emphasize the similarities between LCA and product development processes. A clustered assessment strategy is introduced, segmenting the LCA into partial assessment based on life cycle stages and respective data needs in the development process. A case study for the development of a rotor of an electric motor is conducted to exemplify the implications of the methodology.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The resulting V-model-based methodology for scheduling LCA within product development presents a novel approach that uses the product development process itself as the basis for LCA integration, explicitly addressing the temporal dimension and enabling early, cluster-specific assessments along the product development process. The V-model for LCA presents a step towards LCA-centred product development processes, aligning the two procedures by splitting LCA into three clusters based on development steps. The case study partially shows the applicability of the scheduled application of LCA during product development for two of the three clusters. Hotspots for the design of the developed rotor for an electric motor in the impact category climate change were identified in the raw material acquisition stage, especially the magnets (about 91% of impact).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By providing a methodology for the integration of LCA in the V-model, the study supports practitioners in making informed decisions that reflect environmental impacts, ultimately contributing to more sustainable designs. The conducted work contributes to the advancement of ecodesign frameworks by merging LCA with established product development processes as described in VDI/VDE 2206, thereby fostering a holistic approach to sustainable innovation. It thus contributes to the advancement in process oriented LCA frameworks.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: The overlooked impact of materials’ reference service life on the whole-building life cycle assessment results
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Life cycle assessment (LCA) offers a robust framework for evaluating the environmental impacts of a building throughout its entire life cycle, from material extraction to end-of-life. A key source of uncertainty in LCA is the reference service life (RSL) of building materials, particularly non-structural components, which are often overlooked compared to structural elements. This study aims to examine how the RSL of non-structural materials influences the LCA results of different building types.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study addresses this objective by developing a RSL database for non-structural building materials, based on North American Environmental Product Declarations (EPDs). It prioritizes components that exhibit high variability and explicitly considers their RSL in LCA calculations, which are frequently ignored or replaced with default values in detailed LCA modeling. The database was applied to three representative residential building architypes, single-family (SF), row house (RH), and multi-unit residential building (MURB), assuming a 75-year lifespan as the baseline and varying it between 60 and 90 years. Material quantities for the SF and RH models were obtained from detailed BIM models, while the MURB model used standard quantities from a bill of materials (BOM).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results reveal that underestimating the RSL of a single high-impact component can significantly alter embodied greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in the B4 module. For example, assuming the highest replacement rates for the non–structural materials increase total LCA results by 35–37% for SF and RH buildings, and by approximately 19% for MURB. Moreover, extending building lifespan from 60 to 90 years can further change wbLCA results increased by about 47% and 58% for SF and RH, and 23% for MURB.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings highlight the critical need for accurate and standardized RSL data. It is recommended that policymakers require the inclusion of verified RSLs in EPDs, supported by product-specific testing or modeling. Additionally, the development of region-specific, open-access RSL databases would help reduce uncertainty, improve comparability, and ultimately enable more accurate assessments and reliable life cycle-based decision-making.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: The nuts and bolts of publishing in the International Journal of Life Cycle Assessment
A Global Consensus Life Cycle Impact Assessment Method (GLAM): impacts on human health
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Millions of humans worldwide die prematurely or live with reduced quality of life, partly attributable to pollutant emissions along product, service and technology life cycles, including greenhouse gas emissions, and exposure to air pollutants and toxic chemicals. However, while many of these factors are considered in currently available life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) methods, other aspects affecting human health as a central area of protection in LCIA are currently incomplete or missing. This includes impacts in occupational environments and nutrition-related impacts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The Global Life Cycle Impact Assessment Method (GLAM) was developed as a comprehensive and consensus-driven LCIA method, with methodological documentation and guidance on GLAM human health impact categories provided in the present study. For human health, GLAM proposes indicators for climate change, fine particulate matter (PM
                      <jats:sub>2.5</jats:sub>
                      ) impacts, human toxicity and ionizing radiation that are also available in other LCIA methods as well as for work environment impacts, water scarcity impacts, and lifestyle impacts related to nutrition and physical activity as novel impact categories.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Beyond the introduction of new impact categories, GLAM provides innovation related to differentiating short- and long-term climate change impacts, exposure to indoor and spatialized outdoor PM
                      <jats:sub>2.5</jats:sub>
                      sources, coupling exposure from chemical life cycle emissions and chemicals in products and introducing reproductive/developmental effects for human toxicity, and building on the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study series for the exposure-response and severity assessment across most considered impact categories. GLAM version 1 was released publicly end of 2024.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While GLAM impact characterization factors can be used in life cycle assessment and environmental footprinting, they still require extensive testing in practical studies. GLAM ultimately contributes to achieving health-related targets set in the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals as well as in the Global Framework on Chemicals.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Racial discrimination remains a pervasive social issue but is not systematically addressed in current social life cycle assessment (S-LCA) frameworks. Existing guidelines cover general discrimination only under the subcategory
                      <jats:italic>equal opportunities/discrimination</jats:italic>
                      for the stakeholder group
                      <jats:italic>worker</jats:italic>
                      , which is insufficient, as racial discrimination can occur across supply chains and affect multiple stakeholder groups.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study reviewed S-LCA guiding documents and databases to assess current coverage and to identify gaps. Based on these findings and incorporation of interdisciplinary evidence on racial discrimination from e.g., labour psychology and healthcare, indicators were developed for workers, value chain actors, local communities, and children. They were then reviewed by international racism experts and adapted based on their feedback.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>38 expert-reviewed indicators assessing racial discrimination in S-LCA were proposed and grouped into two sets: a core set representing minimum compliance with anti-racist practices and an advanced set incorporating aspirational measures aimed at addressing systemic racism. A set of reference scales was developed to facilitate implementation for practitioners. The set can be adapted to specific systems under study and local contexts. Methodological and practical challenges remain, including survey design, site-specific data availability, and risks of underreporting.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This work provides the first comprehensive framework for integrating racial discrimination into S-LCA using the reference scale approach and highlights the central role of organisations in addressing racial inequities across supply chains. Next steps include the testing and optimisation of the reference scales in practical application across various sectors and geographical contexts. Future work should expand this foundational work and cover racial discrimination within the impact pathway approach.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

Best practices for comparative LCA of bio-based alternatives to fossil-based products
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Substituting fossil-based products with bio-based alternatives is crucial for a sustainable bioeconomy. Comparative Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) studies can provide valuable guidance on when and how the substitution is environmentally sound. However, careful consideration of technical, regulatory, and economic conditions is needed when performing such LCA studies. The present work aims to identify the best practices for conducting a comparative LCA of bio-based products intended to substitute fossil alternatives in five sectors: construction, packaging, textiles, chemicals, and woodworking.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study is based on two literature reviews, one focusing on the identification of the key challenges in the substitution, and the other reviewing several comparative LCA studies to assess to what extent those challenges were accounted for in the analysis. The findings are used to derive recommendations for multiple stakeholders, primarily for LCA practitioners.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our analysis shows that while some types of bio-based products exhibit the same technical characteristics as their fossil-based counterparts, others present technical differences as well as differences in durability, and availability. Moreover, bio-based materials frequently require compensatory measures to achieve the same technical performance, such as exterior coatings in packaging. Overlooking those challenges in the comparative LCA can lead to biased comparisons.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A thorough accounting of the specific contextual conditions is needed in LCA studies comparing bio-based products versus fossil-based counterparts. Specific recommendations for best LCA practice are provided, by ISO phase, e.g., a clear functional equivalence specification and ensuring that the system boundaries include all activities needed to compensate for differences in functionality. Further quantitative and qualitative research on how following these recommendations can influence the adoption of bio-based products over fossil counterparts is recommended as well.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Advancing environmental assessment of recycled resources: the role of product declarations and circularity metrics in green(er) steel
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While Environmental Product Declarations (EPDs) provide a standardised Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) framework, standard end-of-life (Module C & D) interpretations can obscure the critical value of circularity for products with high recycled content. This paper proposes using circularity metrics as complementary measures to bridge this gap and set benchmarks driving competitive progress toward green(er) production. Consequently, the study asks: How can EPD-aligned LCA be methodologically extended with circularity indicators to provide a transparent, reproducible and comparable assessment of recycled resources, thereby establishing a rigorous basis for defining green(er) steel?</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To establish a performance baseline (RQ1) and benchmark against industry (RQ2), scrap-based electric-arc-furnace (EAF) steel production was assessed using operational data from the industry partner. Moving beyond static hotspot analysis to optimise material and energy selection, the study identifies the electricity emissions intensity threshold required to substantiate a green(er) performance claim. As an illustrative case for recycled resources, the assessment framework was then methodologically extended (RQ3) by calculating the Material Circularity Indicator (MCI) and Circularity Index (CI) using life cycle inventory data. These metrics are integrated alongside standard end-of-life modules to provide a more complete interpretation of the impacts and benefits of resource circularity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Assessing how recycling reduces environmental impacts from resource-intensive industries is essential. Producing one tonne of secondary steel generated under 360 kgCO₂e (cradle-to-gate), satisfying current ‘green’ benchmarks. By providing standalone, reproducible circularity metrics (MCI 0.93; CI 0.60), the proposed methodology confirms a strong inverse relationship between circularity performance and embodied carbon. However, the analysis of these circularity metrics exposes critical end-of-life allocation loopholes and trade-offs where high circularity does not intrinsically guarantee a lower environmental footprint. These results validate the framework, demonstrating that circularity indicators provide a necessary counterbalance to ‘circularity at any cost,’ generating transferable lessons for assessing recycled resources beyond steel.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Advancing EPD methodology requires clearer communication of the quality and utility of resource recovery. To operationalise this, the study recommends procurement specifications mandate both an EPD and a concise circularity statement – explicitly disclosing the MCI, CI, and recycled input percentage. This approach establishes a necessary ‘accountability’ guardrail, ensuring that the value of resource recovery is defined by its ability to operate within sustainable ecological limits rather than mass alone. Ultimately, this research suggests that linking EPD-aligned LCA with product-level circularity indicators can play a more strategic role in supporting global carbon reduction strategies by transparently articulating performance improvements across supply chains and between life cycles.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Life cycle energy, environment, and economic audit of BEV, HEV & ICEV powertrains in India
Life cycle assessment of European cultivated peanuts: evaluating sustainability across different peanut products
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The present work aims to assess and provide valuable insights in the environmental sustainability of three different peanut-based products, namely peanut milk, peanut butter, and peanut oil, produced from European cultivated peanuts via performing a Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>LCA was performed based on the ISO 14040:2006 and 14044:2006 series with ReCiPe 2016 (Hierarchist, H) being selected as the impact assessment methodology.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Based on the obtained results, peanut milk exhibited the best environmental performance, followed by peanut butter and peanut oil. Specifically, the lowest carbon footprint of 0.183 kg CO
                      <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                      eq. per kg of product was evaluated for the case of peanut milk, followed by peanut butter and peanut oil (2.196 and 4.358 kg CO
                      <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                      eq. per kg of product, respectively), with the environmental hotspots differing among the products. For peanut milk, packaging was the main contributor to climate change, while in peanut butter production, roasting and drying were the dominant hotspots due to their high thermal energy demand. Finally, roasting, mechanical processing, and refining due to their high energy and water requirements were identifies as the environmental hotspots of peanut oil.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings indicate that European cultivated peanuts and their derived products can be characterized as environmentally sustainable, particularly under optimized processing conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Life cycle assessment in urban planning: a systematic review of applications and decision-support potential
Environmental Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) of a Peruvian alpaca sweater with a focus on improvement pathways for the alpaca farm phase
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Growing demand for sustainable textiles has renewed interest in natural fibers such as alpaca. So far, sustainability assessments for those fibers are scarce.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Hence, this study assessed environmental impacts of an alpaca fiber sweater across its whole life cycle (farm, factory and distribution (F&D), use, end-of-life) using life cycle assessment. The main goal was to assess the current status quo, identify hotspots and, based on these, to develop farm‑phase improvement pathways. The functional unit was defined as one sweater weighing 303 g. Economic allocation was applied to deal with multi-outputs present in the farm and F&D phases. The farm phase takes place in Peru, as does the production of the sweaters, which are then shipped to Europe, where the use and end-of-life take place. Environmental Footprint version 3.1 was used as impact assessment method.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The farm phase was identified as one of the primary contributors to environmental impacts, particularly in categories such as Climate Change expressed as Global Warming Potential (GWP). Improvement scenarios for the farm phase revealed that a 10% reduction in the enteric fermentation emission factor could significantly improve environmental performance. Increasing the shearing rate by 10% can reduce GWP by over 10%.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study emphasizes the need for high-quality, region-specific data to improve the accuracy of the assessment. Overall, critical insights into the environmental performance of alpaca fiber and improvement strategies for enhancing the sustainability of an alpaca supply chain are provided.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Circular futures of the cement and concrete industry in the European Union: enriching prospective life cycle assessment with participatory foresight
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Given the urgency of the cement and concrete industry to decarbonise by 2050, circular economy (CE) strategies are becoming more eminent. This study aims to identify how CE practices can contribute to lowering environmental impacts and in particular greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in the European Union. As future developments of our socio-economic systems are inherently uncertain, the analysis also considers the effectiveness of CE measures in different types of decarbonised futures.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As part of a prospective LCA (pLCA), the study defines a status quo, a future baseline scenario with a decarbonised energy system and an ambitious circular economy scenario. These are then assessed using the Environmental Footprint (EF 3.1) method for the years 2030 and 2050. To account for the inherently higher epistemic uncertainty in 2050, the ambitious CE scenario is subjected to a sensitivity analysis consisting of four normative socio-economic scenarios on the green transition. The quantification of these alternative future narratives is achieved by means of a stakeholder workshop and sensemaking session. In a final step, the results of the pLCA following the historical trajectory and the ones of the alternative futures are compared and contextualised with the agency of the involved actors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Results indicate that the ambitious CE scenario saves up to 43 Mt CO
                      <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                      -eq. compared to the decarbonised baseline scenario, underlining the substantial contribution of CE to decarbonisation. These savings are mainly due to CE practices related to
                      <jats:italic>reduce</jats:italic>
                      (33% of decrease) strategies. Meanwhile,
                      <jats:italic>reuse</jats:italic>
                      (8%) and
                      <jats:italic>recover</jats:italic>
                      (3%) strategies are less effective, given the high annual inflow of construction materials compared to the outflow. The sensitivity analysis addressing epistemic uncertainty increases the robustness of these results, as CE practices in all alternative futures show higher GHG savings than merely decarbonising the energy system. Moreover, narratives containing shrinking economies match or supersede the GHG savings of the default ambitious CE scenario. The discussion on agency then underlines the importance of a strong state and financial incentives to ensure the implementation of
                      <jats:italic>reduce</jats:italic>
                      practices.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>CE practices are readily available technologies that can support decarbonisation beyond the frequently suggested carbon capture and storage. pLCA scholars, policymakers and practitioners are advised to include more contextualised and diverse socio-economic scenarios in their assessments, based on structured narratives and a participatory process. Such scenarios enable the analysis of uncertainties that go beyond data uncertainty propagation and capture the agency of affected actors who ultimately need to implement the identified solutions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Lithium–sulfur battery technology presents a promising pathway for advancing the electrification of sustainable public transportation systems
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Public transportation plays a crucial role in reducing traffic congestion, greenhouse gas emissions, and social inequalities in urban systems. However, selecting the most sustainable transit bus technologies remains challenging because socio-economic conditions, geographic characteristics, and energy infrastructures vary across regions. This study aims to develop an integrated sustainability-based decision-making framework to evaluate and optimize alternative-fuel bus technologies across different urban contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study proposes a novel sustainability-integrated multi-objective decision-making (SI-MODM) framework that uniquely combines three integrated components: 1) an activity-based life-cycle sustainability assessment model incorporating a battery upscale cost model for an emerging and understudied advanced solid-state battery technology, 2) systematic embedding of region-specific operational and socio-economic context across different dimensions (e.g. driving cycles, urban geography, etc.), and a multi-objective optimization model for strategic fleet planning. This integrated approach enables the first comprehensive evaluation of advanced solid-state lithium sulfur (ASSLiS) batteries for urban transit applications alongside conventional alternatives (diesel, hybrid, compressed natural gas (CNG), and battery electric buses (BEBs) powered by ASSLiS and lithium-ion nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC-LIB) batteries). Real-world driving cycles from four major U.S. cities, such as Atlanta, Chicago, Denver, and New York, were incorporated to capture region-specific operational conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results indicate that BEBs powered by ASSLiS batteries demonstrate the lowest life-cycle carbon emission intensity among all alternatives. In addition, ASSLiS-powered BEBs achieve, on average, 2.5% lower life-cycle costs compared to BEBs powered by conventional LIB batteries. Across all cities analyzed, the ASSLiS BEB consistently appeared in the optimal fleet composition solutions generated by the multi-objective optimization model. The findings also reveal that urban geographic and demographic characteristics significantly influence the life-cycle sustainability performance of alternative-fuel bus technologies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The proposed framework provides a robust analytical tool for policymakers and transit agencies to support sustainable fleet planning decisions. The results suggest that advanced solid-state lithium–sulfur battery technologies offer significant environmental and economic advantages for urban bus electrification. Moreover, the study highlights the importance of incorporating region-specific operational and socio-economic factors when evaluating sustainable public transportation technologies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Assessing environmental impacts of large electric and autonomous tractors in Europe
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The use of diesel fuel in global agriculture causes over 40 megatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalents every year, highlighting the need for more sustainable alternatives. While electrification and automation of agricultural machinery represent promising pathways for sustainable farming, their environmental performance remains underrepresented. This study investigates whether electrification and automation of large agricultural machinery, both individually and in combination, can reduce the environmental footprint of agriculture.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A cradle-to-grave life cycle assessment evaluates four tractor configurations: diesel and electric tractors, each with manual and autonomous operation. The analysis covers the manufacturing, maintenance, use, and end-of-life (EoL) phases over a 15-year lifetime and applies the Environmental Footprint 3.1. method, assessing 16 impact categories. In the use phase, different farm sizes and operating speed scenarios are analysed across the field activities of ploughing, sowing, and spraying. The analysis focuses on the 100-year global warming potential (GWP) to assess the effects on climate change.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Electric tractors can reduce GWP by 56–57% over the entire lifetime, despite substantially higher manufacturing burden. Autonomous operation can provide a further 4–7% reduction in GWP across all scenarios. For operations with high draft force, a reduction in operating speed from 7 km/h to 3 km/h can decrease GWP by 11% per hectare, while extending the cultivated area per battery charge by 18%. The environmental benefits of electrification and automation become most apparent when operated with electricity generated from renewable energy sources at high utilisation rates, to offset the environmental burden from manufacturing and EoL treatment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The electrification and automation of large agricultural machinery offer high potential to transform the environmental profile of agriculture, particularly for contractors and large landowners. Ongoing decarbonisation of electricity supply and advances in battery technology will further reduce GWP in the future. Taken together, electrification and automation can become complementary enablers for a more sustainable agricultural sector.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Comparative life cycle assessment of hydrogen–natural gas blending in residential heating networks for cold climate regions
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study presents a technical and environmental assessment of decentralized green hydrogen production for blending into existing natural gas networks to meet residential heating demand in cold-climate regions. The proposed system integrates photovoltaic (PV) energy, a proton exchange membrane electrolyzer (PEMEL), reverse osmosis water purification, multi-stage compression, and seasonal hydrogen storage.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A dynamic model of the system is developed in MATLAB/Simulink using Simscape, enabling high-resolution simulations of hydrogen production, buffering, compression, and distribution processes over one year. Real thermal demand data from Ronzo-Chienis, a municipality in the Autonomous Province of Trento (Italy), are used as the primary case study. The hydrogen production plant is modelled using site-specific solar irradiance data and local thermal demand profiles, accounting for both daily and seasonal variability. Two hydrogen-blending scenarios (S1: 10% and S2: 20% by volume) are evaluated for system performance, technical feasibility, and environmental benefits. A Life Cycle Assessment is conducted following ISO 14040/44 standards using SimaPro Craft v10.2, comparing the hydrogen-based heating system with a conventional natural gas supply (business-as-usual scenario, 100% CH₄).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results show that increasing the share of H₂ up to 20% could lead to a reduction in 12 out of 18 impact categories, with benefits of 2–20%. Compared with the business-as-usual scenario, the scenario with 10% hydrogen would avoid 27.6 kg CO₂ eq/MWh, while the scenario with 20% hydrogen would avoid 54.9 kg CO₂ eq/MWh, showing a proportional and more pronounced reduction in the other impact categories as well. For example, S2 would lead to reductions in stratospheric ozone depletion and land use (− 18%), marine eutrophication and terrestrial acidification (− 17%), ionizing radiation and freshwater eutrophication (− 14%). Considering the energy demand of Ronzo-Chienis, the introduction of H₂ is estimated to result in an annual reduction of approximately 440–875 t CO₂ eq (435–865 kg per capita), accompanied by further reductions in overall environmental impacts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Overall, the combined results of dynamic modelling and LCA indicate that the introduction of hydrogen into domestic heating systems in Alpine regions could represent a credible pathway for the decarbonisation of residential energy systems, particularly in contexts characterised by harsh winters and high heating demand. Under such conditions, integrating hydrogen into the domestic energy mix could significantly reduce emissions, as even modest improvements in efficiency may translate into substantial seasonal emission savings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Addressing life cycle inventory data gaps for industrial hemp products and processes
Life cycle assessment of a generative artificial intelligence system: the case of a radio application
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI), and particularly generative AI (GenAI), has expanded rapidly in recent years. Although its environmental impacts might be significant, they remain poorly understood and the application of life cycle assessment (LCA) to AI technologies remains in its early stages. The aim of this study is to quantify the life cycle climate impact of an AI-generated radio station named KSPR, marking the first LCA of a system composed of a variety of AI models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this study, LCA is applied to assess the climate impact of KSPR, which is a research prototype of an AI-generated autonomous radio application developed at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm. The functional unit was defined as one hour of generating, broadcasting and streaming radio content. Data was obtained from real-time energy measurements, publications by AI model developers and scientific literature. Sensitivity and scenario analyses were applied to test the reliability of the results and to assess parameter as well as model uncertainties.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In the baseline scenario, computer hardware production is identified as the main contributor to KSPR’s life cycle climate change impact (at about 70%), followed by the use of the text-to-speech conversion model Tortoise TTS (about 10%) and streaming (about 9%). Within the computer hardware category, the screen and graphical processing unit contributed significantly. Sensitivity and scenario analysis revealed significant variability in total results and in the hotspots identified depending on assumptions regarding e.g. computer lifetime, number of users of AI models and training parameters.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions and recommendations</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To the knowledge of the authors, this study provides the first LCA of a composite GenAI system. The findings from this study demonstrate that e.g. computer hardware and inference with Tortoise TTS are key contributors to GenAI applications such as KSPR, while the magnitude of their impacts is highly sensitive to assumptions and data availability. Strategic choices in AI model development, e.g. by reconsidering training practices, and extending hardware lifetimes can reduce impacts. The results emphasise the importance of improved data transparency on AI development for e.g. hardware, training resources, model lifetimes and usage statistics, to enable more accurate and comparable LCAs. This is also important in the context of the LCA methodology applied, such as for allocating impacts of AI model training to specific AI services. Continued advancement of LCA of AI is critical for developing a more complete understanding of the sustainability of AI systems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
